passages.t: Peace with God, and hope that does not disappoint
passages.happening:
“Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 1). Through him we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, “And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God” (verse 2).

“Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance” (verse 3); perseverance produces character, and character produces hope (verse 4).

“And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
‘Therefore’ marks a turn. Chapters 1 to 4 showed how a person is set right with God. Now Paul shows what that means for life.

‘Peace’ was a word with a political ring in Rome. The emperor Augustus had presented himself as the bringer of peace to the world, and coins and monuments celebrated the Roman peace. Paul speaks of a deeper peace: not a truce imposed by a conqueror, but the end of hostility between people and God.

‘Access’ could describe being brought into a king's presence. Believers have been brought in, and they ‘stand’ in grace. It is not a door they must keep forcing open.

‘Rejoice’ is the Greek word for boasting. In 3:27 boasting was shut out. Here it returns, but now the boast is in God's hope, in hardship, and in God himself (verse 11).

The chain in verses 3 and 4 moves step by step: suffering, then perseverance (holding on under weight), then character (the quality of something tested and proved true, like metal tried in fire), then hope. Paul's hearers in Rome knew hardship. Some were probably slaves. Some had been driven from their homes under Claudius. Paul does not tell them to pretend.

Verse 5 brings the Holy Spirit into the argument. He was named only briefly before (1:4; 2:29); in chapter 8 he will fill the page. God has not only declared his love; he has ‘poured’ it into believers' hearts.
passages.ot:
Isaiah joined righteousness and peace: “The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever” (Isaiah 32:17).

‘Hope does not disappoint’ echoes the Psalms. Of Israel's fathers David says, “they trusted in You and were not disappointed” (Psalm 22:5).

The pouring out of the Spirit was promised by Joel: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28).
passages.hard:
‘Suffering produces perseverance’ is true, and it is also one of the verses most often used carelessly. Paul is describing what God can bring out of hardship over time, in the life of a believer held by his love. He is not saying that suffering is good, or that people in pain should feel glad about it. It is never a line to hand to someone in fresh grief or pain, as if it answered their loss.

If you are suffering now, your pain is real, and you are not failing God by feeling it. The psalms are full of people who cried out to God. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). Please do not carry it alone: talk to someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The site's Honest Answer, ‘If God is good, why is there so much suffering?’, faces the larger question.
passages.asks: Paul says believers have peace with God and stand in grace. Ask whether you live as one who stands, or as one always afraid of being thrown out. Then think of a hardship you have come through. Ask, gently, what God built in you there, and whether you can see any hope that grew from it.

passages.t: ‘While we were still sinners, Christ died for us’
passages.happening:
“For at just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly” (verse 6).

“Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die” (verse 7). “But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (verse 8).

If we have been justified by his blood, how much more will we be saved from wrath through him (verse 9). “For if, when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!” (verse 10).

“Not only that, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Greek and Roman stories praised people who died for a friend, a benefactor or their city. Paul's hearers would agree that someone might dare to die for a good man. What no one expected was a death for enemies. That is the point of verse 8: God's love is shown not to people who deserved it, but to people who were against him.

‘Powerless’, ‘ungodly’, ‘sinners’, ‘enemies’. Paul piles up four words to describe us before Christ. Each is worse than the one before.

‘How much more’ is a way of arguing that Jewish teachers used, from the greater to the lesser. If God did the harder thing, dying for his enemies, how much more will he do the easier thing, keeping those who are now his friends.

‘Reconciled’ was the word for making peace between parties who had been at war, or friends who had fallen out. In Paul's world the weaker side usually sought peace from the stronger. Here the injured party, God, makes peace with those who wronged him, and pays the cost himself.

Notice ‘saved through His life’. Jesus's death reconciles; his risen life keeps us. The good news does not stop at the cross.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's servant suffers for those who had wandered from God: “We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

God's love for the undeserving runs through the prophets. Through Hosea he says of Israel, which had turned away, “I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them” (Hosea 14:4).

‘Saved from wrath’ looks back to the wrath of God in 1:18 and the ‘day of wrath’ in 2:5. The prophets spoke of the day of the LORD as a day of wrath (Zephaniah 1:15).
passages.hard: Does ‘justified by His blood’ mean God the Father had to be persuaded to love us? Paul says the opposite. The love comes first: “God proves His love for us in this” (verse 8). The cross does not change God's heart toward us; it shows it. At the same time Paul says that we are ‘saved from wrath’ through Jesus (verse 9), so the cross also deals with a real problem between us and God. Christians explain how these fit in more than one way, as the note on 3:21-26 sets out. All agree that the initiative is God's, and that his love is not bought.
passages.asks: Paul says Christ died for us while we were still God's enemies. Ask whether you believe God loves you only when you are doing well. Then ask who your enemies are, and what it would mean to make the first move toward peace, as God did.

passages.t: Sin and death through one man
passages.happening:
Paul now looks at the whole human story through two men.

“Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned” (verse 12).

Sin was in the world before the law was given, he says, but sin is not counted up when there is no law (verse 13). “Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed. He is a pattern of the One to come” (verse 14).

Paul starts a comparison in verse 12 and breaks off to explain it. He finishes it in verses 18 and 19.
passages.hearers:
‘One man’ is Adam, the first man in Genesis. Paul does not name him until verse 14. He wants his hearers to hold two figures side by side: the one man through whom sin came, and the one man, Jesus, through whom grace came.

Sin and death are pictured as powers. Sin ‘entered’ like an intruder. Death ‘reigned’ like a king. Paul is not only talking about wrong acts and the end of a life. He is talking about two rulers that took over the human race.

Jewish writers near Paul's time also thought about how Adam's sin affected his children. Later Jewish books, such as 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, lament that Adam's sin brought death to all, while still holding each person responsible.

Verse 13 and 14 answer a puzzle. Between Adam and Moses there was no written law. Adam broke a clear command; later people did not have one. Yet people still died. So sin and death were at work even where there was no law to break.

‘A pattern of the One to come’. The Greek word is typos, a mould or a stamp. Adam is like a shape that points ahead to Christ. Both are heads of a whole humanity. What one did affected all who belong to him.
passages.ot:
Genesis tells of the one command: “you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die” (Genesis 2:17). After Adam and Eve ate, God said, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).

Genesis 5 then repeats the same words of one generation after another, beginning with Adam: “and then he died” (Genesis 5:5). Death reigns, as Paul says.

Paul draws the same comparison in another letter: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).
passages.hard:
What does verse 12 teach about how Adam's sin affects us? The churches answer in different ways.

The Western churches, Catholic and Protestant, following Augustine, teach that all humanity shares in Adam's fall, so that every person is born with a fallen nature and a share in Adam's guilt. This is called original sin. Some stress that humanity was really present in Adam; others, especially Reformed Christians, that Adam acted as humanity's appointed head. The Orthodox churches speak rather of ancestral sin: through Adam, all inherit death and a nature bent toward sin, but not Adam's guilt.

There is also a question of translation. The last words of verse 12, ‘because all sinned’, were read in the Old Latin Bible as ‘in whom all sinned’, meaning in Adam, and Augustine built on that reading. Most modern translations, like the BSB, have ‘because’. Many who use ‘because’ still hold that we are bound up with Adam's sin.

Was Adam one historical man, and how does this relate to what science says about human origins? Paul's argument rests on Adam and Christ as heads of two humanities. Christians differ on how that relates to human origins: many hold that Adam was a real first man; others read Genesis 1 to 3 differently while holding to Paul's point. These notes take no position on the details. The site's Honest Answer, ‘How should a Christian read Genesis 1?’, sets out the views. On every view, all have sinned, and Christ is the remedy.
passages.asks: Paul says sin and death reign over the whole human race. Ask where you see that reign: in the world, in your family, in yourself. Then notice that Paul says it to get to Christ. Adam is only ‘a pattern of the One to come’. Ask whether you think more about the damage, or about the one who came to undo it.

passages.t: The gift is not like the trespass
passages.happening:
“But the gift is not like the trespass” (verse 15). If many died by the trespass of one man, how much more did God's grace, and the gift that came by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, overflow to the many (verse 15).

One sin brought judgment and condemnation; but the gift followed many trespasses and brought justification (verse 16). If death reigned through one man, how much more will those who receive God's abundant grace and gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ (verse 17).

“So then, just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men” (verse 18). “For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (verse 19).

The law came in so that the trespass would increase, “but where sin increased, grace increased all the more” (verse 20), so that, as sin reigned in death, grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The comparison Paul began in verse 12 is completed here, but it is never equal. Again and again he says ‘how much more’. Adam's act did great harm. Christ's act does far more good.

Notice the numbers. One sin by Adam led to condemnation. Christ's gift came after many sins, not one, and still brought justification. Grace does not just match the damage. It overtakes it.

‘Reign’ appears again and again. Death reigned. Now those who receive grace will ‘reign in life’. The picture is of a change of kings. Under Adam, death ruled. Under Christ, grace rules, and believers share his rule.

Verse 19 sets Adam's disobedience against Christ's obedience. Adam took what was forbidden. Christ obeyed all the way to the cross.

Verse 20 would have startled Jewish hearers. The law ‘came in so that the trespass would increase’. Paul means that when sin is named by a clear command, it shows up as open rebellion, as he said in 4:15. The law did not create sin, but it showed how deep it went. And where sin grew, grace grew more.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's servant is the one whose obedience makes many righteous: “By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities” (Isaiah 53:11). Paul's ‘the many will be made righteous’ (verse 19) echoes it closely.

Adam's disobedience is told in Genesis 3: the woman “took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it” (Genesis 3:6).

The law came through Moses at Sinai (Exodus 20), long after Adam. Paul's ‘from Adam until Moses’ (verse 14) covers that whole stretch of Genesis.
passages.hard:
Who are ‘the many’ and ‘all men’ in verses 18 and 19? Does Paul mean that everyone will in the end be saved? Christians read these verses in different ways.

Some, called Christian universalists, take ‘all’ in the same full sense on both sides: as all died in Adam, so all will finally be made alive in Christ. Some Christians, from early times to today, have held or hoped for this; most churches have not taught it.

Reformed readers usually say that ‘all’ on the Christ side means all who belong to him, those in Christ, just as ‘all’ on the Adam side means all who belong to Adam. They point to verse 17: grace reigns in ‘those who receive’ it.

Arminian and Wesleyan readers usually say that Christ's act really was for all people, so that grace reaches out to everyone and is offered to everyone, but that each person must receive the gift by faith to be saved.

These notes set out the readings and do not choose. All agree on what Paul stresses: grace is greater than sin, and God's gift is far larger than the damage. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Is hell forever, or does it end?’, takes up the related questions.
passages.asks: ‘Where sin increased, grace increased all the more’. Ask what sin you think is too big for grace. Then read verse 20 again. Paul is not saying sin does not matter. He is saying it cannot outrun grace. Ask what it would mean to live under grace as your king, and not under guilt.
